rules.rule: A file with no content is a valid configuration whose body has no attributes and no blocks
A file with only spaces, tabs or inline comments, and no newline, has an empty body
Blank lines are ignored before, between and after the items of the top-level body and of block bodies, and in bodies with no items (disputed)
A line comment on a line of its own is ignored like a blank line in a body (disputed)
Spaces before an item at the start of its line are ignored
The top level of a file is a body without enclosing braces, so a brace cannot open or close it
A body, at the top level or in a block, can mix attributes and blocks in any order
An attribute is a name, an equals sign and an expression, with any number of spaces between them and after the value
An attribute name is exactly one bare identifier: not a quoted string, a number, a traversal, an index or two identifiers
An attribute without a name before its equals sign is an error
A single equals sign must follow an attribute name; a missing sign, a colon or == is an error, and an identifier alone is not a body item
An attribute without an expression after its equals sign is an error, at the end of a line or of the file
An attribute's name, equals sign and the start of its value must be on one line
A newline outside brackets ends an attribute, so the next line cannot continue its expression, while newlines inside brackets don't end it
Nothing but whitespace and comments can follow an attribute's value on its line, so neither another attribute nor a comma can
A line comment or an inline comment can follow an attribute's value; a line comment ends the attribute like a newline, and an inline comment spanning lines doesn't, though a newline after it does
The end of the file can take the place of the newline after the last attribute (disputed)
Parsing keeps an attribute's expression for the application to evaluate later, so evaluation errors are not parse errors
Attributes inside blocks, at any depth, are evaluated like top-level attributes, and an error in one of them makes evaluation fail
A block's labels don't define variables, so an expression in the block's body cannot refer to a label
An attribute name can be defined only once in a body, whatever the values and whatever comes between the definitions, in the top-level body and in block bodies
Attribute names are unique within a body in the information model, so a native body, at the top level or in a block, that defines a name twice is an error
Uniqueness applies to each body separately, so a parent body, a nested block body and sibling block bodies can each define the same name
A block has zero or more labels, quoted or bare in any mix, kept in source order
A block type is a bare identifier, which may contain dashes, and cannot be a quoted string or a number
A block label is a quoted string or a bare identifier (which may contain dashes and non-ASCII letters); a number, a single-quoted string, a traversal, an operation or a heredoc is an error
A quoted label can be empty or contain any text, including non-ASCII characters and characters that mean something outside strings, but not a literal newline
A quoted label keeps its code points as written, without Unicode normalization (disputed)
Escape sequences in a quoted label are decoded, and a backslash sequence that is not one of them is an error
A quoted label cannot contain interpolations or directives, while a $ or % that starts no sequence is text
In a quoted label, $${ and %%{ are read as the text ${ and %{, while $$ and %% not followed by { stay as written
No whitespace is needed between a block's type, quoted labels and opening brace
A block's type, labels and opening brace are on one line; a line comment ends that line, while inline comments spanning lines are whitespace
An equals sign between a block's labels and its opening brace is an error
A multi-line block's opening brace is followed by a newline, which a line comment provides and an inline comment spanning lines doesn't, and the body after it can be empty
A multi-line block's closing brace follows the newline that ends the body's last item, so it cannot share that item's line, though it can be indented
A newline or a line comment must follow a block's closing brace, so no other item can follow on that line
The end of the file can take the place of the newline after the last block's closing brace (disputed)
A block, multi-line or one-line, needs a closing brace before the end of the file
A block's body can contain blocks, including one-line blocks, to any depth
A body can contain any number of blocks of one type, including with identical labels or with different numbers of labels
The blocks of a body form a sequence in source order
A one-line block has a header, then braces on the same line around nothing or one attribute, with or without spaces
The attribute value in a one-line block can be any expression, including one with braces, a template or brackets spanning lines
Inline comments, even ones spanning lines, are whitespace inside a one-line block
A one-line block holds at most one attribute, so a second attribute or a comma after the first is an error
A one-line block cannot contain a nested block
The content of a one-line block must be a whole attribute: a bare name, an equals sign and a value
A block whose opening brace is followed by an attribute on the same line must close right after that attribute, with no newline or line comment in between, which rules out a heredoc value
Attribute names and block types are separate, so an attribute and a block can share a name in either order, and a block's body can define an attribute named like the block
An equals sign after a name makes an attribute, so name = { ... } is an attribute with an object value
CR LF works as the newline that ends attributes and follows block braces
A body's content is reached by giving a schema of the attributes and blocks the application expects

rules.rule: A body schema that requests a block type with the same name as a requested attribute is an error
